summary: Describes use cases, with directions and interpretations, for organizations and relying parties that create or encounter RPKI object scenarios in the public RPKI, discussed in relation to Internet routing. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A guide of examples showing what to do with the digital ownership papers for internet addresses, whether you issue them or check them.

subtitle: A guide to creating and interpreting RPKI digital authorizations for route origins.

tldr.problem: Internet routers accept route announcements from any autonomous system (AS) without checking if the origin AS actually owns the IP prefix being announced. Attackers can announce prefixes they do not own, hijacking traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is a cryptographic system where prefix owners create Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) that digitally sign which ASNs are authorized to originate routes for specific IP prefixes. Routers can then validate that a route announcement is authorized before accepting it.
tldr.outcome: ISPs and network operators can validate BGP announcements and reject forged route origins. The RFC documents practical examples of how organizations create ROAs for their resources, handle multi-homing, manage partial deployments, and interpret validation results.

facts.label: AS 0 ROA meaning
facts.value: Prefix should not be announced from any ASN

today: RFC 6907 is an Informational RFC published in March 2013 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the primary documentation for how organizations should create and interpret ROAs. As of 2013, RPKI deployment was growing among major ISPs and network operators to prevent BGP route hijacking.

sections.title: Route Origins and BGP Hijacking
sections.content:
BGP is the routing protocol that tells routers where to send packets. A route announcement carries a prefix (like 10.1.0.0/16) and the origin AS claiming to originate that route. Today, routers accept any announcement with any origin AS, even false ones.

RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) is a system of digital certificates that proves ownership and authorization. A prefix owner creates a Route Origin Authorization (ROA), a signed statement saying "ASN 64496 is authorized to announce 10.1.0.0/16". Routers verify the signature and accept only authorized announcements.

This document describes scenarios where organizations create ROAs for their prefixes and ASNs, and how routers validate incoming BGP routes against those ROAs.
sections.eli5: BGP is like a bulletin board where anyone can write 'I own this network.' RPKI is like putting a lock on the bulletin board so only the real owner can update their entry. This RFC explains how to use the lock and how to check it.

sections.title: Creating ROAs for Your Resources
sections.content:
An organization that has been allocated IP prefix 10.1.0.0/16 and owns ASN 64496 must create a ROA to say 'ASN 64496 is authorized to originate 10.1.0.0/16.' The ROA contains three pieces: the ASN, the prefix, and a maxLength field that limits how specific the prefix can be.

If the organization wants to announce both 10.1.0.0/16 and more-specific routes like 10.1.1.0/24, it sets maxLength to 24, meaning prefixes up to /24 are allowed. If it wants to permit only the /16 itself, it sets maxLength to 16.

The RFC documents many real-world scenarios: an organization that wants to restrict announcements (using an AS 0 ROA saying 'no ASN should announce this'), multi-homed customers delegated parts of an allocation, and organizations that have received prefixes from an upstream provider.
sections.eli5: When you get an IP address range, you sign a document saying which network number can announce it and how specific the announcements can be. It's like saying 'my company, network 64496, can announce my range in pieces down to /24.'

sections.title: How Routers Validate Routes
sections.content:
When a router receives a BGP route announcement with a prefix and origin AS, it looks for a covering ROA. The ROA is a covering ROA if its prefix is a less-specific or exact match to the route prefix.

The router checks three things: does a covering ROA exist, is the route prefix within the maxLength limit, and does the origin AS in the route match the ASN in the ROA. If all three match, the route is Valid. If a covering ROA exists but one of the three conditions fails, the route is Invalid. If no covering ROA exists, the route is NotFound.

A special case is the AS 0 ROA, which says 'no ASN should originate this prefix.' Any route matching an AS 0 ROA is Invalid. Similarly, a ROA can authorize a prefix to be announced only up to a certain length; more-specific prefixes are Invalid.
sections.eli5: A router asks 'is there a signed permission for this announcement?' and 'does the permission allow it?' If yes to both, the route is valid. If no permission exists, the router is unsure. If permission says no, the route is blocked.

sections.title: Partial Deployment and Transfers
sections.content:
Not all organizations deploy RPKI at the same time. An organization might issue RPKI certificates for its own prefixes but its upstream provider has not yet adopted RPKI. This creates a hierarchy problem: RPKI is strictly hierarchical, so a child cannot issue ROAs if the parent does not participate.

When prefixes transfer between organizations (e.g., from ISP A to ISP B), there is a transition period. The RFC recommends that the new owner issue a ROA before advertising the prefix, and issue it with lead time, so that when validation software encounters the route, the new ROA is already in the cache. Otherwise, old ROAs from the previous owner may still be valid and mark the new owner's announcements as Invalid.

Multi-homed organizations, which have multiple upstream providers, can delegate sub-allocations to customers and issue ROAs on their behalf, allowing those customers to originate their own routes from their own ASNs.
sections.eli5: When companies gradually adopt RPKI or when an IP range changes owners, there are tricky timing issues. The RFC explains when to issue new permissions and how much lead time you need so routers accept your announcements instead of rejecting them.

sections.title: Design Principles for RPKI
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes a 'make before break' principle: assume a route is authorized unless proven otherwise by an explicit ROA that forbids it. This is important for partial deployment, where some networks use RPKI and others do not.

Because ROAs take time to propagate to all relying parties, organizations should publish ROAs before advertising new routes. This applies when receiving a new allocation, acquiring a prefix in a transfer, or delegating to a customer. Publishing first ensures routers receive the authorization before they see the announcement.

The document also notes that a prefix holder need not originate routes from their own ASN; they can authorize any ASN to originate their prefix. This is useful for outsourcing or when a provider announces an aggregate on behalf of multiple customers.
sections.eli5: Key design ideas: trust by default unless a permission explicitly says no, publish your permissions before using them, and allow delegating to other networks.
